title: Can a USD 10/month membership fund cent-scale tipping and payouts without becoming a payment processor?
summary: Provider-hosted UI parts with a custom frontend (Stripe Payment Element, Checkout, Connect; merchant-of-record options), a prepaid balance ledger vs per-tip charges (card fees make a 1-cent charge impossible), stored-value and money-transmission risk, refunds, chargebacks, tax, payouts, marketplace revenue share.

title: Stripe domestic US card fee: 2.9% + $0.30 per successful charge
summary: Base rate for online card payments within the US, confirmed on Stripes own pricing page. This is the floor cost any per-transaction model (membership charge or per-tip charge) has to clear. Fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Stripe Billing adds 0.7% of billing volume (pay as you go) or a flat plan starting near $620/month
summary: Stripe Billing is a separate overlay fee on top of the base card fee, for subscription management. Pay-as-you-go is 0.7% of billing volume with no recurring charge; the alternative is a monthly-contract plan starting around $620/month. Fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Computed: a $10/month subscriber costs about $0.66/month (6.6%) in Stripe fees before retries
summary: Card fee 2.9%*10 + $0.30 = $0.59, plus Billing pay-as-you-go 0.7%*10 = $0.07, totals about $0.66/subscriber/month. At 1,000 subscribers thats about $660/month; at 10,000 subscribers about $6,600/month. Excludes failed-payment retries, currency conversion, disputes. Computed from stripe.com/pricing rates, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Paddle (merchant of record) charges a flat 5% + $0.50 per checkout transaction, no monthly fee
summary: All-inclusive fee covers payments, billing, global tax compliance (VAT/sales tax registration and remittance), fraud protection, and support. Confirmed on Paddles own pricing page, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Lemon Squeezy: 5% + $0.50 per transaction flat, plus surcharges (international, PayPal, recurring)
summary: Merchant-of-record fee bundles tax compliance in. Primary pricing page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; number confirmed instead across several independent 2026 aggregator reviews that agree exactly (dodopayments.com, getstacksmart.com), fetched 2026-09-04. Recheck against lemonsqueezy.com/pricing directly before relying on it.

title: Polar (merchant of record) Starter plan: 5% + $0.50/transaction as of 2026; cheaper rate needs a paid plan
summary: Polar restructured pricing in 2026 from a flat 4% + $0.40 to a tiered model: free Starter plan is now 5% + $0.50. The old ~4% economics require a paid plan ($20 to $400/month) or a grandfathered pre-2026-05-27 account. Chargeback fee is $15. Confirmed on polar.sh/docs, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Stripe Connect Express: $2/active-account/month + 0.25% + $0.25 per payout sent
summary: An account is active in any month payouts are sent to it. Cross-border payouts add roughly 0.25%+ of volume; instant payouts add 1%. On top of this, connected-account charges still pay the base 2.9%+$0.30 card fee. Confirmed on stripe.com/connect/pricing, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: stripe-node needs an explicit fetch-based HTTP client to run on Cloudflare Workers
summary: Default stripe-node client uses node:https, unavailable on Workers. Fix: pass httpClient: Stripe.createFetchHttpClient() when constructing the client. node_compat is no longer required since stripe-node v11.10.0. Confirmed via github.com/stripe/stripe-node issue 1593 and Stripes own stripe-samples/stripe-node-cloudflare-worker-template repo, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Webhook verification on Workers uses constructEventAsync() with a WebCrypto CryptoProvider, not constructEvent()
summary: Node cryptos synchronous constructEvent() needs node:crypto, unavailable on Workers. Stripes own stripe-samples/stripe-node-cloudflare-worker-template repo verifies signatures with await stripe.webhooks.constructEventAsync(body, signature, secret), backed by createSubtleCryptoProvider(). Fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Idempotency keys protect Stripe API calls only, not webhook re-delivery
summary: Stripes idempotent-request mechanism dedupes retried POSTs to the Stripe API. It does nothing for a webhook handler invoked twice by Stripes own retry system; Stripes docs explicitly say to track processed event IDs in your own store and not rely on event ordering. Confirmed on docs.stripe.com/webhooks, Handle duplicate events and Event ordering sections, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Stripe enforces a $0.50 USD minimum on every charge so its own fee cannot exceed the charge
summary: Stated directly on Stripes currencies page: Stripe enforces a minimum payment amount for all charges to make sure the Stripe fee doesnt exceed your charge. This is a hard platform-wide floor, not a configurable setting. Fetched 2026-09-04.

title: A true 1-cent per-tip charge is impossible on Stripe; even the $0.50 floor loses 62% to fees
summary: At the minimum charge ($0.50), Stripes fee (2.9%+$0.30 = about $0.31) consumes 62% of the charge. A genuinely new, individually-authorized 1-cent or 10-cent real-money tip charge cannot clear the card networks fixed-fee floor at all. Computed from stripe.com/pricing + docs.stripe.com/currencies, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Flattr (2010s) solved cent-scale tipping by never charging per click
summary: Users prepaid a monthly budget (e.g. 5 euro). Clicking a Flattr button that month split that one prepaid charge evenly among everything clicked, minus a 10% platform cut, settled once a month. No individual micro-charge ever happened. Confirmed across freesoftwaremagazine.com, techcrunch.com and forbes.com historical coverage, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Mediums Partner Program pays writers from a subscriber-funded pool, never per-clap charges
summary: Money comes from member subscription fees pooled monthly, then divided among writers by engagement (originally clap count, later reading time plus claps and highlights). No individual reader-to-writer charge ever occurs. Confirmed on help.medium.com Partner Program earnings calculation page, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Stripe Radar velocity rules are the standard defense against card-testing at low charge amounts
summary: Card testing (checking stolen numbers are live) shows up as rapid low-dollar charges from one IP or card. Radar supports rules like block if authorized charges per card exceed N per hour. A real per-tip charge model at cent-to-dollar scale is exactly the pattern card testing mimics, so this defense is load-bearing for model (d). Confirmed on docs.stripe.com/disputes/prevention/card-testing and docs.stripe.com/radar/rules, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Model (b), monthly allocation from the $10, is the only tipping model with no new charge floor problem
summary: This much of your $10 is yours to give never charges anything new; it just marks part of an already-collected $10 as spendable. It sidesteps the $0.50 minimum-charge floor entirely. The cost moves from processing fees to legal risk: it only stays simple if the allocation is strictly non-refundable and never cashable out, because a cashable balance is what triggers stored-value/money-transmission law (see stored-value findings below). My own synthesis; no external url.

title: Model (c), aggregate tips into one periodic real charge, is the only model where a NEW dollar clears cent-scale
summary: Flattr/Medium-style pooling lets a tip be genuinely new money (not pre-paid membership) while still clearing the card-fee floor, because the real charge only happens once a period, batched. Trade-off: payout is delayed a full period, and refunds/chargebacks apply to the whole batched charge, not one tip, so per-tip dispute handling gets harder to reason about. My own synthesis.

title: Model (a) prepaid balance and model (d) per-tip-above-$1 are the two Stripe can charge cleanly, but differ in who is exposed
summary: (a) fund $10, spend in cents keeps a spendable balance on the platforms books between charge and tip -- the stored-value exposure this whole question is about. (d) per-tip charges only above $1 needs no balance at all: every tip is its own real-time Stripe Connect charge, clearing the fee floor, with the platform never holding money between charge and payout. (d) is the lowest-legal-risk of the four models; its cost is that tipping stops feeling like a like at low levels. My own synthesis.

title: FinCENs closed-loop exemption caps at $2,000/device/day and requires redemption with a defined merchant
summary: Prepaid access usable only for goods/services from a defined merchant or set of locations, capped at $2,000 or less loaded per device per day, is excluded from FinCENs prepaid program definition -- no MSB registration, AML program, or SAR filing required. Above the cap or outside those bounds it IS a prepaid program with full BSA obligations. Confirmed via Federal Register 2011-19116 and FinCENs own prepaid-access FAQ, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: FinCENs closed-loop definition is redemption with a merchant, not transfer to another person
summary: FinCENs own FAQ defines closed-loop strictly as usable only for goods or services in transactions involving a defined merchant or location, and its examples (toll roads, campus cards, retail chains) are all user-redeems-with-merchant patterns. It does not mention, and does not resemble, one user sending value to another user -- the exact shape of an in-platform tip. Confirmed on fincen.gov, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: 49 US states plus DC require a money-transmitter license for holding and moving stored value between users
summary: All states except Montana require licensure for an entity that receives money or monetary value for transmission to a third party, or sells/issues stored value. Multiple licensing-guide and state-regulator sources name the peer-to-peer-transfer element specifically (not just redemption) as the trigger for platforms where users hold balances and send them to other users. Aggregated across state regulator pages (e.g. dfpi.ca.gov) and licensing-consultancy guides, fetched 2026-09-04; no single state statute read verbatim, hence contested on exact wording.

title: FinCENs payment-processor exemption covers only processing through BSA-regulated clearance systems, not a held balance
summary: 31 CFR 1010.100(ff)(5)(ii)(B) exempts an entity that facilitates payment for goods/services through a clearance-and-settlement system (e.g. ACH) intermediating solely between BSA-regulated financial institutions. It does not cover a platform holding a discretionary, spendable customer balance between charge and use. Confirmed via Cornell Law LII CFR text and FinCEN administrative ruling FIN-2014-R009, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Stripe Connect keeps platforms out of possession/control of funds, shifting the regulatory burden to Stripes own license
summary: Funds settle to Stripes own safeguarding/e-money-licensed accounts before payout to the seller and platform; Stripe designed Connect this way specifically so platforms do not need their own payment license. Stripe states over 4,000 European platforms rely on this instead of obtaining their own license. Confirmed on Stripes PSD2/Connect guide, fetched 2026-09-04. Note: this claim is Stripe-authored and framed around EU PSD2 -- see skeptic-pass entry below on its US applicability.

title: EU e-money issuance needs an EMI license: EUR 350,000 minimum capital, rising with 2% of outstanding e-money
summary: EMD2 (Directive 2009/110/EC) sets the EMI capital floor at 350,000 euro (down from 1 million pre-EMD2), maintained at the greater of that floor or 2% of average outstanding e-money. A small-EMI exemption exists per Article 9 for average outstanding e-money under 5 million euro plus other conditions. EMD2 is being folded into PSD3. Aggregated across EMI-license consultancy guides (advapay.eu, codegotech.com), fetched 2026-09-04; not the directive text itself, hence contested on exact conditions.

title: Stored-value balances are subject to state unclaimed-property (escheatment) law once dormant, typically 3-5 years
summary: Gift-card-like balances usually escheat to the state of the owners last known address (or the holders state of incorporation if unknown) after a dormancy period generally 3-5 years, with rules on percentage, expiration and fees varying sharply by state. Non-transferable platform credit with no cash value is exempt in some states, not others. Aggregated from practitioner summaries (bakertilly.com, alston.com), fetched 2026-09-04; not primary state statute text, hence contested.

title: The briefs literal $10-becomes-a-tipping-balance idea reads as money transmission, not a closed-loop gift card
summary: If that balance can be sent to OTHER USERS (not just redeemed for the platforms own paid content), it is peer-to-peer value transfer, which closed-loop specifically excludes -- closed-loop means redemption with the issuing merchant, not with another customer. A design where every tip is instead its own real-time Stripe Connect charge/transfer, with no platform-held balance ever sitting between charge and payout, is what keeps the platform outside that definition. Synthesis of the FinCEN and money-transmitter findings above, not itself independently checkable at one url -- credence contested rather than established for that reason, despite high personal confidence.

title: Does a non-cashable balance that only multiplies a real, simultaneous Stripe charge escape stored-value rules?
summary: A hybrid: a non-refundable, non-transferable reputation credit spendable only as a multiplier on a real per-tip Stripe Connect charge the user authorizes at the moment of sending (never held as an independent balance, never itself sent to a person) might dodge both the charge-floor problem and the money-transmission definition. No source found addresses this specific fact pattern; every finding here reasons by analogy from plain gift cards and generic P2P-app guidance. This needs paid counsel in the states of operation, not more web search -- the single most useful open item in this log.

title: Destination charges put the platform on the hook for Stripes fee/dispute risk; separate charges and transfers decouple charge from payout
summary: Destination charges route the full charge onto the platforms own Stripe balance first, then transfer a split to the connected account -- the platform pays the Stripe fee and bears dispute liability on that charge. Separate charges and transfers decouple the charge and payout in time, which Stripe recommends for marketplaces splitting one purchase across multiple sellers. Confirmed on docs.stripe.com/connect/charges and docs.stripe.com/connect/integration-recommendations, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Cloudflare D1 serializes all writes to one database through a single SQLite instance
summary: Each D1 database processes queries single-threaded; throughput is bound by query duration (about 1,000 qps at 1ms/query, 10 qps at 100ms/query). One D1 database (not sharded per-user) already gets total write ordering for free, without needing a Durable Object. Confirmed on developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/limits, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Independent Cloudflare-storage writeups argue Durable Objects, not D1, are the better default for a financial ledger
summary: Several third-party Cloudflare-architecture comparisons (not Cloudflares own docs) argue DOs strict per-entity serializability is the correct fit for balance-tracking, versus D1s single-database (not single-entity) consistency. The briefs own premise of D1-for-the-ledger is not the uncontested default in the wider Cloudflare-dev literature. Aggregated from inventivehq.com and architectingoncloudflare.com, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: An append-only double-entry ledger needs uniqueness and one atomic multi-row insert, which one D1 database already gives you
summary: Never UPDATE a balance row; only INSERT balancing debit/credit pairs and derive balance via SUM. That needs a UNIQUE constraint (idempotency key) and one transaction per tip, not a long-held per-account lock -- both already provided by a single D1 database. Durable Objects extra guarantee (per-entity serializability beyond one DBs total order) only starts to matter if the code computes balance via read-then-write instead of SUM-on-read. My own synthesis; no source addresses this specific append-only framing directly.

title: Stripe charges a flat $15 dispute fee per US chargeback regardless of outcome; contesting adds a $15 counter fee if you lose
summary: Standard $15 dispute fee applies whether you win or lose. Since 2025-06-17, an additional $15 counter fee applies if you contest and lose (refunded if you win, so winning a contest still costs the original $15). Confirmed via chargeback-recovery vendor coverage (chargeflow.io) cross-checked against docs.stripe.com/disputes context, fetched 2026-09-04; exact dollar figures come from a vendor blog, not a Stripe pricing page, hence flagged rather than pure primary.

title: In the US, 3D-Secure/SCA is optional and off by default; a US-only membership can ship without it
summary: Stripe states US cards are not enrolled in 3DS unless the merchant explicitly requests enrollment -- unlike the EU/UK where SCA is close to mandatory. A US-only $10 membership can launch without a 3DS step, at the cost of shifting more fraud/dispute liability onto the merchant. Confirmed on Stripes Strong Customer Authentication docs, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: EU PSD2 lets card payments under 30 euro skip 3DS step-up, but resets after 5 low-value payments or 100 euro cumulative
summary: Low-value exemption: transactions under 30 euro can be processed frictionlessly. The exemption resets and full SCA is required again after 5 consecutive low-value exempt payments on one card, or 100 euro cumulative, whichever comes first. Relevant only if EU-issued cards pay membership/tips. Aggregated from PSD2-compliance vendor docs (checkout.com, solidgate.com), fetched 2026-09-04; not the RTS regulatory text itself, hence contested on exact figures.

title: Stripe splits declines into soft (retry later) and hard (need a new card) -- the two need different user-facing messages
summary: insufficient_funds and generic_decline are soft declines, safe to retry later without new card details. lost_card and invalid_cvc are hard declines requiring the customer to enter new card details immediately. A single generic your card was declined message loses this distinction that Stripe itself recommends acting on. Confirmed on docs.stripe.com/declines/card, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Federal 1099-K threshold for 2025 and later is back to $20,000 and 200+ transactions
summary: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 reversed the ARPA phase-down (which was headed to $600 with no transaction minimum by 2026) and restored the pre-2021 threshold of $20,000 AND more than 200 transactions for third-party network payments. Card-network payments have no minimum threshold at all. State thresholds can be lower and are not preempted. Confirmed directly on irs.gov, page last reviewed 2026-06-28, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Apple App Store: 30% standard, 15% under $1M/year (Small Business Program), resets to 30% for the rest of the year if crossed
summary: Small Business Program cuts commission to 15% for developers under 1 million dollars annual proceeds; crossing that line snaps the account back to 30% for the remainder of that calendar year. Subscriptions separately drop to 15% automatically once a subscriber passes their first 12 months, on any account. Aggregated from RevenueCat and TechCrunch coverage of Apples own program terms, fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Creator-subscription platforms (Patreon, Substack) cluster near 10% platform cut before Stripe fees, landing 13-16% all-in
summary: Patreon consolidated to a single 10% standard fee in 2025; Substack charges every writer the same 10%. Both add Stripes own 2.9%+$0.30 (plus 0.5% recurring on Substack) on top, landing near 13-16% of gross. Gumroad charges 10%+$0.50 on direct sales, 30% on marketplace-discovered sales. Aggregated from creator-platform-fee comparison sites, fetched 2026-09-04; no primary Patreon/Substack pricing page read directly, hence contested on exact current figures.

title: An 80/20 creator/platform split sits above the creator-subscription norm but well below app-store norms
summary: 10 to 16 percent all-in is the Patreon/Substack norm; 30 percent is the app-store norm. 20 percent lands between them, defensible specifically if that cut is understood to cover payment processing AND moderation/hosting/discovery of paid content, not just subscription billing -- closer to what Apples pre-2021 bundled 30 percent covered before it split out a separate processing line. My synthesis of the two findings above, genuinely arguable rather than settled.

title: What do content-specific marketplaces (Udemy, Skillshare) charge creators, versus general subscription platforms?
summary: Not dug in this pass. The briefs marketplace question is about premium learning modules specifically, which is closer to a course marketplace than a Patreon-style subscription -- Udemy and Skillshare revenue-share terms were not looked up and would sharpen or undercut the 80/20 defense above.

title: For a one-person company, a merchant-of-record may beat Stripe+Connect despite costing more per transaction
summary: Paddle/Lemon Squeezy/Polars flat 5%+$0.50 (about 2-3 points above Stripes unbundled 2.9%+$0.30) may still be worth it for a solo owner because it buys away global sales-tax/VAT registration and remittance and merchant-of-record liability entirely, work a one-person company is least equipped to do itself. Genuinely arguable -- my own theory, not the mainstream default choice; see the following opinion for the counter-case.

title: Mainstream answer to the MoR theory: Stripe Tax narrows the premium once volume and audience are mostly US
summary: Stripe Tax (a bolt-on percentage fee) handles US sales tax and EU VAT registration/remittance for less than the MoR premium at real volume, and Stripe Billing plus Connect already cover subscriptions and payouts in one stack. The MoR case is strongest for a genuinely global, VAT-exposed audience from day one; weaker if the MVP audience is mostly US, which the brief assumes. Synthesis of findings on Stripe Billing/Connect fees above, not itself independently checkable at one url, hence contested not established.

title: Boundary line A: reading/browsing free, creating/publishing gated behind the $10 membership
summary: Simplest to build (auth-gate write paths only) and matches the briefs much stays free instruction, but risks looking stingy if even basic profile/follow actions require payment. My own candidate line, one of three; no external url.

title: Boundary line B: core topics free, AI-assisted or compute-heavy features (generation, video, live) gated
summary: Ties the $10 price to actual marginal cost (inference/compute), the clearest why $10 story to a paying user, but requires metering usage per user before the MVP can even decide the line. My own candidate line, one of three; no external url.

title: Boundary line C: everything free up to a generous usage/rate limit, $10 removes the limit
summary: Lowest friction to try the product, matches Medium-style freemium norms, but makes the free tiers limit itself an early design/tuning problem instead of a one-time gate decision. My own candidate line, one of three; no external url.

title: Overall MVP recommendation: no stored-value/tipping-balance mechanism at all on day one
summary: Ship the $10/month Stripe Billing membership (Payment Element + Customer Portal) only. Defer tipping until it can be a real Stripe Connect charge per tip above a $1 floor (model d) or a periodic pooled payout (model c) -- both never require the platform to hold a balance, so no MSB/e-money exposure exists on day one. Matches the briefs own section 25 instruction to not implement tipping until understood. Synthesis of every finding in this log, not independently checkable at one url, hence contested not established.

title: Skeptic pass: Stripes no-license-needed Connect claim is EU-PSD2-framed marketing, not a US money-transmission ruling
summary: Stripes platforms do not need their own license framing is Stripe-authored content, written for the EU PSD2 context specifically, not a neutral regulator confirming the same holds for US state money-transmission law, which is 50 separate state regimes with no single federal preemption. Treat the earlier Stripe Connect/PSD2 finding as strong evidence for the EU e-money side only, not a blanket Connect always keeps you license-free claim for the US.

title: Skeptic pass: the Paddle/Lemon Squeezy/Polar fee snapshot is dated and the market visibly repriced within 2026
summary: All three merchant-of-record percentages here are a September 2026 snapshot in a market that repriced mid-year (Polar changed its headline rate from 4%+$0.40 to 5%+$0.50 during 2026). Do not treat these percentages as stable inputs to a financial model without a re-check at build time.

title: Skeptic pass: no primary source directly analyzes a membership-fee-partly-convertible-to-tipping-balance fact pattern
summary: No statute, FinCEN ruling, or state regulator opinion letter was found that directly addresses this exact design. Every finding here reasons by analogy from plain closed-loop gift cards and generic P2P-app money-transmitter guidance, not from a ruling on this specific shape. An actual answer needs paid counsel, not more web search -- this is the same crux as the earlier open question, restated after the skeptic pass confirms nothing closed it.
